engine: Seismometer 0.5.0 (Epic, open source): Agresti–Coull and Hanley–McNeil intervals; likelihood ratios by the log method

reports.title: Systolic murmur detector (heart sounds)
reports.question: Does this child have a heart murmur that an expert would annotate?
reports.intendedUse: Research and teaching: point a learner or reviewer to recordings likely to contain a systolic murmur. Not a screening or diagnostic test.

population.text: 873 children and adolescents (with a recorded murmur status) from two mass screening campaigns in Paraíba, Brazil (CirCor DigiScope 1.0.3), up to four valve sites each; 68 with murmur status “unknown” excluded. Consecutive screening, not a referred population.

reports.reference: Murmur presence, location, timing and Levine grade as annotated by the CirCor dataset’s expert annotators, per valve. The detector never saw these labels.
reports.indexTest: Automatic: mean systolic-to-diastolic energy ratio over resolved beats ≥ 2.5 × that of a murmur-free child of the same age band at the same valve, with a heart rate plausible for age. Flagged at any valve = patient positive.
reports.independence: External: the threshold was set before CirCor was added and has not been changed on it.

metrics.label: Sensitivity
metrics.explain: children with an annotated murmur correctly flagged

metrics.label: Specificity
metrics.explain: children without it correctly left unflagged

metrics.label: PPV
metrics.explain: flags that were correct, at this sample’s prevalence

metrics.label: NPV
metrics.explain: negatives that were correct, at this sample’s prevalence

metrics.label: Prevalence in the sample
metrics.explain: changes PPV and NPV; sensitivity and specificity do not depend on it

extra.label: ROC AUC of the underlying ratio (per valve, threshold-free)
extra.explain: 0.5 = chance, 1 = perfect. Shows the feature carries real signal even where the fixed cut-off misses.

bedside: Of 100 patients who have the finding it flags about 40; of 100 who do not, it wrongly flags about 1.
A positive flag raises the odds a lot — often decisive (LR+ 27.53): when it flags a murmur, it is usually right.
A negative result barely changes the odds (LR− 0.61): it cannot rule a murmur out.
It finds loud murmurs and misses soft ones: grade I/VI 18 %, grade III/VI 89 %. Soft murmurs are the ones screening most needs.
limits: Children only; adults were not tested.
Infants are poorly served (fast heart rate leaves too little diastole to separate S1 and S2).
Innocent and pathological murmurs are not distinguished — the reference is “murmur present”, not structural disease.
Heart-sound segmentation finds about 71 % of S1/S2; beats it cannot resolve cannot be scored.
reports.verdict: Rule-in aid for research review; not usable to exclude a murmur.

reports.title: Adventitious breath-sound detector — children (SPRSound)
reports.question: Does this breath (event) contain an adventitious sound — wheeze, rhonchus, stridor or crackle?
reports.intendedUse: Research and teaching: highlight where on a recording adventitious sounds probably are. Not a diagnostic test.

population.text: 3188 expert-annotated breath events in 677 recordings of the 191 browsable SPRSound children (Shanghai Children’s Medical Center, Yunting stethoscope).

reports.reference: Per-event labels (normal, wheeze, rhonchi, stridor, fine/coarse crackle) by SPRSound physicians.
reports.indexTest: Automatic tonality (wheeze/rhonchus) and transient (crackle) detectors against the patient’s own normal site, shipped thresholds.
reports.independence: Development data: these thresholds were tuned on SPRSound. The figures are optimistic — the KAUH result below is the honest estimate on new patients.

metrics.label: Sensitivity
metrics.explain: expert-labelled adventitious breath events correctly flagged

metrics.label: Specificity
metrics.explain: events without it correctly left unflagged

metrics.label: PPV
metrics.explain: flags that were correct, at this sample’s prevalence

metrics.label: NPV
metrics.explain: negatives that were correct, at this sample’s prevalence

metrics.label: Prevalence in the sample
metrics.explain: changes PPV and NPV; sensitivity and specificity do not depend on it

metrics.label: Continuous sounds (wheeze, rhonchi, stridor) recognised as continuous

bedside: Of 100 patients who have the finding it flags about 51; of 100 who do not, it wrongly flags about 17.
A flag raises the odds a little (LR+ 2.96); a clean result barely changes the odds (LR− 0.59).
Continuous sounds are recognised more reliably than crackles.
limits: Tuned and tested on the same database (see independence).
Short clips (9–15 s) from one hospital and one stethoscope.
Event-level figures; events from one child are not independent, so the intervals are too narrow.
reports.verdict: Teaching aid; its accuracy here is an upper bound.

reports.title: Adventitious breath-sound detector — adults (KAUH)
reports.question: Does this adult’s recording contain an adventitious sound?

population.text: 112 adolescents and adults 12–90 y (King Abdullah University Hospital, Jordan; 3M Littmann 3200): 35 healthy, 77 with asthma, heart failure, COPD, pneumonia, fibrosis and others. One chest site each.

reports.reference: Whole-recording sound label from the KAUH dataset’s clinical annotation (normal, wheeze, crackles, …); no event timings.
reports.indexTest: Same detectors and thresholds as SPRSound, unchanged; diaphragm mode is the primary result.
reports.independence: External: a different country, age range and stethoscope, thresholds untouched.

metrics.label: Specificity
metrics.explain: healthy adults without it correctly left unflagged

metrics.label: PPV
metrics.explain: flags that were correct, at this sample’s prevalence

metrics.label: NPV
metrics.explain: negatives that were correct, at this sample’s prevalence

metrics.label: Prevalence in the sample
metrics.explain: changes PPV and NPV; sensitivity and specificity do not depend on it

bedside: Of 100 patients who have the finding it flags about 64; of 100 who do not, it wrongly flags about 43.
A flag barely changes the odds (LR+ 1.48); a clean result barely changes the odds (LR− 0.64): on a different stethoscope it is weak in both directions.
Crackles — the sign of heart failure and fibrosis — are found in only 23 % of recordings that have them.
limits: Small: 35 healthy adults, so specificity is imprecise.
Filter mode changes the result substantially; per-device recalibration is open work.
reports.verdict: Does not generalise to the Littmann 3200 without recalibration.

reports.title: Apnea / hypopnea and AHI from breath sound (overnight)
reports.question: How many apneas and hypopneas per hour does this sleeper have, and in which severity class?
reports.intendedUse: Research only: estimate an acoustic AHI from a long breath-sound recording. Not a substitute for polysomnography or home sleep apnea testing.

population.text: 10 adults referred to a sleep lab for suspected sleep apnea (Athens; PSG-Audio), 44.2 h of diagnostic recording, 1975 scored events. ~89 % of this dataset has severe apnea.

reports.reference: Full polysomnography scored by a sleep technician and a certified physician (AASM rules), using airflow, effort, SpO₂ and EEG. Sound was not used for scoring.
reports.indexTest: The page’s acoustic flow proxy on the tracheal contact microphone; AASM adult rules (≥ 30 % drop for hypopnea, ≥ 90 % for apnea, ≥ 10 s); shipped thresholds.
reports.independence: External, untuned: the scoring was written before these nights were seen.

metrics.label: Event sensitivity
metrics.explain: scored apneas/hypopneas overlapped by an acoustic event

metrics.label: Event PPV
metrics.explain: acoustic events that overlapped a scored event

extra.label: AHI bias (acoustic − PSG), events/h
extra.explain: interval shown = 95 % limits of agreement (Bland–Altman): where one patient’s error will fall

extra.label: AHI rank correlation with PSG (Spearman ρ)

bedside: It finds about 45 of every 100 scored events; about 72 of every 100 events it reports are real.
Its AHI is too low by 26.2 events/h on average, and for one patient the error can be anywhere from -52.1 to -0.2 events/h.
Severity class matched polysomnography in 4 of 10 patients; every miss put the patient in a milder class.
A low acoustic AHI does not exclude sleep apnea.
limits: Pilot of 10 patients — the intervals are wide.
Almost no healthy sleepers: specificity cannot be estimated.
Adults only; the paediatric rule is untested.
No SpO₂ or effort channel: obstructive vs central and desaturation-based hypopneas are out of reach.
Events are clustered within patients; event-level intervals are too narrow.
reports.verdict: Not ready for clinical use; under-counts systematically.

reports.title: Biological-age signal (longevity precondition)
reports.question: Does the sound carry information about a person’s age, so that an “acoustic age gap” could one day be tested as a longevity marker?
reports.intendedUse: Research question only. No longevity, mortality or risk output exists or is implied.

population.text: Held-out patients: 45 KAUH adults, 345 SPRSound children, 345 CirCor children.

reports.reference: Recorded chronological age (KAUH, SPRSound: years; CirCor: age band). No survival or follow-up data exist in any dataset here.
reports.indexTest: Ridge regression on detector features, fit on 60 % of patients, scored on the held-out 40 %.
reports.independence: Held-out split; null model = guess the training mean.

extra.label: Adult age error, years (model vs guessing the mean)
extra.explain: guessing the mean: 17.46 y — no improvement (permutation p = 0.31)

extra.label: Heart rate vs age band (Spearman ρ)
extra.explain: p = 5e-17 — heart rate falls with age, as physiology predicts

extra.label: Heart-rate-for-age deviation, normal vs abnormal outcome (effect r)

bedside: Breath sounds as measured here do not reveal an adult’s age; there is no “acoustic age gap” to interpret.
Heart rate from heart sounds behaves as expected with age in children — a sanity check, not a new marker.
Nothing on this platform estimates longevity or mortality risk.
limits: No outcome data: longevity cannot be validated with any open auscultation dataset available today.

ml.engine: scikit-learn models; Seismometer 0.5.0 metrics, intervals and fairness rule

models.title: Machine-learning murmur model (heart sounds)
models.task: Expert-annotated murmur present vs absent, per patient
models.data: CirCor DigiScope 1.0.3 — children, two Brazilian screening campaigns

comparator.name: shipped rule (sysDia ≥ 2.5× baseline), same test patients

models.note: Fit on training patients only. The rule shown on the patient pages is unchanged; Discoveries 13 still reports the shipped rule on all 941 patients.
bedside: On 350 held-out patients it flags 54.2 % (95 % CI 42.7–65.2) of those with the finding and wrongly flags 10.1 % of those without.

The rule the site uses today, on the same patients: sensitivity 41.7 %, specificity 98.6 %. The model finds more murmurs at lower specificity — a different point on the same trade-off, not a free gain.
Fairness audit (Seismometer rule): Infant (Age band): sensitivity critically lower (×0.25); unknown (Age band): sensitivity higher (×1.31); CC2014 (Screening campaign): sensitivity lower (×0.69).

models.title: Machine-learning adventitious-sound model (breath sounds)
models.task: Expert recording label abnormal (CAS, DAS or both) vs normal, per recording
models.data: SPRSound, all four releases — children, Shanghai, Yunting stethoscope

external.name: KAUH adults, Littmann 3200 diaphragm — model and threshold frozen

models.note: Recording-level; several recordings per child, all in the same split. Release is a known confound (labels and devices drift between releases).
bedside: On 344 held-out patients it flags 40.9 % (95 % CI 37.4–44.5) of those with the finding and wrongly flags 9.0 % of those without.
On adults recorded with a different stethoscope (KAUH) the frozen model reaches AUC 0.713 — sensitivity 22.4 %, specificity 94.3 %.

Fairness audit (Seismometer rule): BioCAS2023 (Release (recording batch)): sensitivity critically higher (×1.55); BioCAS2024 (Release (recording batch)): sensitivity critically higher (×1.51); BioCAS2025 (Release (recording batch)): sensitivity lower (×0.74); 6–17 y (Age group): sensitivity critically lower (×0.37); <1 y (Age group): sensitivity higher (×1.29), specificity lower (×0.76).
